cards.title: Nothing Is Wasted
cards.body: Today changes very little chemically, and that is fine. What changes is the decision. Research finds a specific, written intention outperforms general resolve, and that past failed attempts do not predict failure now. Measure today by the fact that a decision exists.

cards.title: The Shape of an Urge
cards.body: Cravings tend to arrive in waves rather than as constant pressure. Studies across compulsive behaviours find an urge builds, peaks and subsides over minutes rather than hours, provided it is not fed with attention. Each peak you sit through weakens the association slightly.

cards.title: Sleep Gets Its Hour Back
cards.body: If your habit lived late at night, sleep is the first change. Removing screens from the hour before bed reliably shortens how long you take to fall asleep. You may not feel rested yet; months of sleep debt do not clear in three nights.

cards.title: Restlessness Is Normal Here
cards.body: Around now many men report irritability, restlessness, low mood and vivid urges. This comes from self-reports, not from evidence that you were dependent in a medical sense. It is what happens when easy stimulation is removed, and it generally eases within two weeks.

cards.title: The Hours You Got Back
cards.body: One week. The most certain benefit here is arithmetic rather than neuroscience: the time and attention this habit consumed is now available. Reclaimed time is the one benefit nobody disputes. Energy may still feel uneven. Watch what you do with the recovered hours.

cards.title: Cues Start Losing Their Grip
cards.body: Certain cues, a time of day, an empty house, a particular app, fire an urge because they were paired with the behaviour hundreds of times. When the cue appears and the behaviour does not follow, that pairing weakens. The pace varies widely between people.

cards.title: Less Fog, Slightly Sharper
cards.body: Two weeks in, some men notice they can hold attention longer. The likely explanation is unremarkable: better sleep, less late-night stimulation, fewer interruptions. Evidence does link heavy use to attention difficulties, but the direction of cause is genuinely unclear. Do not expect a transformation.

cards.title: The Gap Narrows
cards.body: The distress here comes less from the act than from the gap between how you behave and who you think you should be. Three weeks of acting closer to your values tends to close it, and men commonly describe feeling less at war with themselves.

cards.title: Evidence About Yourself
cards.body: A month gives you proof of your capability. Self-efficacy, the belief that you can execute what you intend, is among the strongest predictors of maintained change, and it is built by experience rather than encouragement. Days you handled badly and recovered from count double.

cards.title: Arousal and Response
cards.body: Around this point some men report changes in sexual response: more responsiveness to a real partner, less reliance on escalating material. The evidence is mostly case reports and self-report surveys, so this is reported rather than proven. Persistent problems deserve a doctor, not an app.

cards.title: How You Are With People
cards.body: Two months. Partners often report noticing before the man does: more presence, less secrecy, less defensiveness. Research links problematic use with lower relationship satisfaction, though those studies are correlational and cannot prove direction. If trust was damaged, repair takes longer than your streak.

cards.title: About the Ninety-Day Reboot
cards.body: You will read that ninety days rewires the brain or resets dopamine receptors. Treat that with suspicion: those claims are not supported by good human evidence, and the ninety-day figure is community folklore, not a research finding. Three months does make a pattern more stable.

cards.title: Energy and Drive, Honestly
cards.body: Many men report more drive and confidence by this stage. But claims that abstinence produces large or lasting testosterone increases are not supported. The one study people cite found a short-lived, modest change. Better sleep, exercise and reclaimed time explain how you feel.

cards.title: Living Closer to Your Values
cards.body: Six months. This stretch is usually where behaviour stops feeling like restraint and starts feeling like character. Values-congruent living is associated with lower distress, though hard to isolate from everything else improving alongside. Men frequently describe an inner quiet. Complacency causes most relapse here.

cards.title: Boredom Stopped Being Dangerous
cards.body: One of the most durable changes men describe is a restored tolerance for being unstimulated: queues, quiet evenings, solitude. That matters, because the reflex to escape discomfort was the engine of the habit. Attention research supports the principle, though the specifics are still being studied.

cards.title: A Year of Evidence
cards.body: A year. You now have first-hand evidence about the kind of man you are under pressure, across seasons, travel, stress and boredom. That predicts what you do next year better than motivation. The habit may still surface occasionally; that is ordinary, not a verdict.
